Campaigns on an immediate moratorium on new data centers.
Campaigns on expanding health care access, including Medicaid expansion and strengthening rural hospitals.

promises.text: Says she will name the affordability crisis an emergency item on her first day so lawmakers can pass the $1,500 refund.
Says that on day one she will fire Education Commissioner Mike Morath and appoint an educator to lead the Texas Education Agency.
Says she will end the STAAR test, pause A-F school ratings and return taken-over school districts to their communities.
Says she will audit and terminate education vendor contracts and redirect the money to make teachers among the highest paid in the nation.
Says she will direct the Public Utility Commission to freeze residential electricity rates until data centers and other large users are required to cover their own costs.
Pledged to veto any partisan gerrymandered maps.

record.text: Voted against SB 2 (2025), the education savings account program, and helped lead House opposition to it.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the school finance bill; was a negotiator of the 2019 school finance law.
Voted against SB 8 (2021), the six-week abortion ban, and HB 1927 (2021), permitless carry.
Voted against SB 14 (2023), the ban on gender transition treatments for minors, and SB 10 (2025), the Ten Commandments display law.
Voted against SB 4 (2023) and SB 8 (2025), the state immigration enforcement laws, and SB 17 (2025), the foreign land purchase restrictions.
Voted for HB 441 (2021) and HB 218 (2023), reducing penalties for low-level marijuana possession, and against SB 3 (2025), the THC ban.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the bail constitutional amendment, and HJR 7 (2025), the dedicated water fund amendment; was recorded absent on SB 9 (2025).
Voted against HB 2127 (2023), the state preemption law, and HB 1243 (2023), which increased the penalty for illegal voting.
Voted against SB 2627 (2023), the electric generation funding bill, and against the House versions of the 2023 and 2025 state budgets.
Joined Democratic quorum breaks in 2021 over the election bill and in 2025 over congressional redistricting; voted against HB 4 (2025), the new congressional map.
Authored a 2025 bill to stop institutional investors from buying more than 10 single-family homes.
Voted for HB 2730 in 2021, which regulated land acquisition by entities with eminent domain authority; it passed the House 143 to 1.

notes.text: The Texas Supreme Court in May 2026 dismissed the attorney general's case seeking removal of House Democrats who broke quorum in 2025.
Hinojosa accepted televised debate invitations, including an October 15 forum; the campaign says Abbott did not respond.

q_prop_tax_eliminate.summary: Proposes ending corporate subsidies and using the savings to cut property taxes, with the end goal of eliminating residential property taxes.

q_vouchers.summary: Voted against the 2025 voucher program, calls it a payout for the privileged and wants to end it.

q_school_funding.summary: Wants Texas teachers to be among the highest paid in the nation and authored the Fully Fund Our Future Act in 2023.

q_ten_commandments.summary: Voted against SB 10 (2025), which requires classroom displays.

q_medicaid.summary: Calls Medicaid expansion a central part of her plan to lower health costs and cover every Texas child.

q_abortion.summary: Supports restoring legal abortion access, including for rape, incest and fatal fetal diagnoses, and voted against the 2021 ban.

q_border_state.summary: Says the state's border spending is wasteful when crossings are at record lows and criticizes no-bid Operation Lone Star contracts.

q_deportation.summary: Says migrants who contribute to their communities should not be rounded up or deported, calls for closing the Dilley family detention center, and voted against SB 8 (2025).

q_gun_laws.summary: Voted against the 2021 permitless carry law.

q_bail.summary: Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment requiring denial of bail in certain felony cases.

q_cannabis.summary: Voted for bills reducing penalties for marijuana possession in 2021 and 2023 and against the 2025 THC ban.

q_fossil_priority.summary: Voted against SB 2627 (2023), which created funding mechanisms for new electric generating facilities.

q_foreign_land.summary: Voted against SB 17 (2025) restricting land purchases by certain foreign entities.

q_water.summary: Voted for HJR 7 (2025), dedicating sales tax revenue to the Texas water fund.

q_voting_access.summary: Says she has filed and supported dozens of bills to expand voting access, including online voter registration and better ballot access for students; this adds her own statement to the earlier record-based stance.

q_election_fraud.summary: Voted against HB 1243 (2023), which increased the criminal penalty for illegal voting.

q_preemption.summary: Voted against HB 2127 (2023), which limits local ordinances.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted against SB 14 (2023), the state ban on gender transition treatments for minors.

q_legal_status.summary: Says longtime, law-abiding residents should have a path to legal status.

q_eminent_domain.summary: Voted for HB 2730 (2021), which added rules for land acquisition by entities with eminent domain authority; the bill passed the House nearly unanimously.

issue_notes.summary: Says Flock cameras have become a tool for warrantless surveillance and should be taken down statewide.
Called on Abbott to suspend the state gas tax and backfill road and school funding from the surplus or Rainy Day Fund.
Supports nonpartisan redistricting and pledges to veto maps gerrymandered to benefit either party.
Proposes stopping private equity firms from buying up single-family homes and holding landlords accountable for AI-driven rent pricing.
Wants an executive order for an immediate data center moratorium and a special session to repeal data center tax breaks.
Says she helped defeat a bill to end prevailing wage requirements, and she is a member of the Communications Workers of America.

In 2019 joined Democratic lawmakers urging a special session on gun violence and said a person with an active murder warrant could legally pass a Texas background check, a claim PolitiFact rated Mostly True.

candidates.name: Pat Dixon
candidates.current_role: Engineer and business owner; Libertarian nominee for governor
candidates.background: Pat Dixon is a process control engineer and president of DPAS Inc. who has worked for companies including Honeywell and Emerson. He holds an engineering degree from Miami University in Ohio. He served on the Lago Vista City Council from 2005 to 2009 and chaired the Libertarian Party of Texas for 10 years. He has previously run for the Texas Senate and Travis County commissioner.

priorities.text: Campaigns on "right sizing government," meaning people can do what they want as long as they do not harm others.
Campaigns on identifying specific state and local spending cuts before promising tax relief.
Campaigns on ending corporate welfare, including tax incentives for AI data centers.
Campaigns on parent and teacher empowerment, including a statewide scholarship that follows each child to any school.
Campaigns on election reforms including approval voting and nonpartisan redistricting.

promises.text: Says that as governor he would refuse to take part in immigration enforcement that harms the life, liberty and property of Texans.
Says that as governor he would decline a presidential request to redraw districts in the president's favor.

record.text: Served two terms on the Lago Vista City Council (2005 to 2009), where he says he worked to reduce spending.

notes.text: Former U.S. Rep. Ron Paul endorsed Dixon for governor in October 2026.
Dixon answered the League of Women Voters (VOTE411) and iVoterGuide questionnaires and posted his responses.

q_prop_tax_eliminate.summary: Is skeptical of promises to eliminate property taxes without detailed spending cuts and cautions against replacing them with sales taxes.

q_min_wage.summary: Opposes the minimum wage, citing Milton Friedman.

q_vouchers.summary: Ideally wants a statewide scholarship giving every child the same amount to follow them to any school, and opposes turning away voucher applicants.

q_abortion.summary: Calls himself pro-life but says he will not impose his religion as governor and that doctors and adults should make difficult medical decisions; disagrees with enforcing the Comstock Act.

q_border_state.summary: Says the governor does not make federal border policy and Texas can cooperate with enforcement, but would refuse cooperation that harms Texans' rights.

q_deportation.summary: Says "if you are peaceful and productive, welcome" and does not support the current means ICE uses to enforce immigration law.

q_legal_status.summary: Says his federal policy would be to welcome peaceful and productive immigrants and that legal immigration is nearly impossible under current law.

q_gun_laws.summary: Defends lawful gun uses, raises due process concerns about red flag laws and opposes broad mental health screening of gun owners.

q_cannabis.summary: Says adults should be free to make their own choices, applauded Abbott's veto of the THC ban and says Texas should go further.

q_fossil_priority.summary: Considers nuclear the best long-term option but prefers that market forces drive energy choices.

q_voting_access.summary: Supports voter verification but says photo ID burdens some eligible voters and suggests biometrics on voter registration cards.

q_preemption.summary: Says he will respect local control.

q_gambling.summary: Agrees with expanding gambling, saying prohibitions are unenforceable.

q_trans_minors.summary: Was neutral, saying he would be reluctant to intervene when parents and child consent under professional supervision but opposes transition without parental consent.

q_ten_commandments.summary: No statement on the classroom display law was found; inferred from his statements that he will enforce separation of church and state as an absolute requirement and that the governor should have nothing to do with religion.

q_election_fraud.summary: No statement on fraud enforcement funding was found; inferred from his statement that Texas elections are conducted properly and produce legitimate results, while he favors paper ballots and hand-verified samples.

issue_notes.summary: Opposes taxpayer incentives for data centers and says growth should pay for itself, but would not oppose centers that pay for their impact.
Says Texas elections are conducted properly and results are legitimate; supports approval voting and nonpartisan redistricting.
Says opening the market to new competitors and lower-cost providers will lower prices.

candidates.name: Dan Patrick
candidates.current_role: Lieutenant Governor of Texas since 2015
candidates.background: Dan Patrick has been lieutenant governor, the presiding officer of the Texas Senate, since January 2015. He previously represented Houston-area Senate District 7 from 2007 to 2015. Before office he was a television sportscaster, conservative talk radio host and radio station owner. He holds a bachelor's degree in English from the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, and won the March 3, 2026 Republican primary with 84.7 percent.

priorities.text: Campaigns on lowering property and business taxes, including larger homestead exemptions.
Campaigns on strengthening the electric grid by adding reliable thermal power.
Campaigns on school choice and what he calls a high-quality education for all.
Campaigns on securing the border and supporting law enforcement.
Campaigns on protecting life, religious freedom and the Second Amendment.

promises.text: Proposes "Operation Double Nickel": raising the school homestead exemption to $180,000 and lowering the age for the senior exemption and tax freeze from 65 to 55.

record.text: Designated school choice (SB 2), a THC ban (SB 3), a $140,000 homestead exemption (SB 4), grid reliability (SB 6) and water supply investment (SB 7) among his top 2025 priority bills.

Designated as 2025 priorities bills requiring local law enforcement to assist federal deportation efforts (SB 8), bail reform (SB 9 and SB 40), Ten Commandments displays in schools (SB 10), stopping non-citizen voting (SB 16) and restricting foreign adversary land purchases (SB 17).
Designated a $200,000 homestead exemption for seniors (SB 23), teacher pay increases (SB 26) and the Life of the Mother Act (SB 31) as 2025 priorities.
SB 2 (vouchers), SB 10 (Ten Commandments), SB 17 (foreign land), SB 8 (ICE agreements) and SB 9 (bail) became law in 2025; SB 3 (THC ban) was vetoed by Gov. Abbott.
Presided over the 2023 Senate impeachment trial of Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Authored the state's mandatory pre-abortion ultrasound law as a senator.
In 2020 offered a reward of up to $1 million for information on voter fraud and called expanded mail voting a scam.
Backed the 2017 bill restricting bathroom use by transgender students, which did not become law.
Called SB 14 (2023), which bars gender transition treatments for minors, one of his top priorities when the Senate passed it.
Did not allow House-passed sports betting and casino amendments to advance in the Senate in 2023, saying there was no support among Senate Republicans.

notes.text: Months before the Paxton trial, the Defend Texas Liberty PAC gave Patrick's campaign a $1 million contribution and a $2 million loan; Patrick had also previously donated to and loaned money to Paxton's 2018 campaign.

In September 2026 Vikki Goodwin filed a police complaint alleging two AI-generated campaign ads depicting her violated the state deepfake law; Patrick's campaign called them obvious parody, denied breaking the law and removed them the next day. No charges had been reported.
Endorsed in the 2026 primary by Donald Trump, Greg Abbott, the Combined Law Enforcement Associations of Texas, Texas Alliance for Life and Texas Gun Rights.
Reported about $24.4 million cash on hand as of Sept. 24, 2026.
Did not respond to the League of Women Voters of Texas questionnaire for its November 2026 voters guide.

q_vouchers.summary: Made school choice (SB 2) one of his top priorities; it became law in 2025.

q_school_funding.summary: Designated a teacher pay increase (SB 26) as a 2025 priority and pushed a $5,000 teacher raise in 2019.

q_ten_commandments.summary: Made SB 10, requiring Ten Commandments displays in classrooms, a 2025 priority; it became law.

q_abortion.summary: Opposes abortion exceptions for rape or incest, with an exception only when the mother's life is in danger; authored the mandatory ultrasound law.

q_border_state.summary: Lists securing the border among his priorities and says border security funding and more state troopers are funded in the budget.

q_deportation.summary: Made SB 8, requiring local law enforcement to assist federal deportation efforts, a 2025 priority; it became law.

q_gun_laws.summary: Called for closing stranger-to-stranger background check gaps in 2019, then backed expanding gun rights including permitless carry.

q_bail.summary: Made bail reform (SB 9 and SB 40) a 2025 priority, describing it as keeping violent criminals off the streets.

q_cannabis.summary: Made a ban on THC products (SB 3) a top priority and says he opposes any path to recreational marijuana.

q_fossil_priority.summary: Says he is working to strengthen the grid by adding reliable thermal power and made grid reliability (SB 6) a priority.

q_foreign_land.summary: Made SB 17, "Stopping Foreign Adversaries' Land Grabs," a 2025 priority; it became law.

q_water.summary: Made SB 7, "Increasing Investments in Texas' Water Supply," a 2025 priority; it became law.

q_voting_access.summary: Called expanded vote-by-mail a scam in 2020 and presided over the 2021 election law.

q_election_fraud.summary: Offered up to $1 million for voter fraud tips in 2020 and made stopping non-citizen voting (SB 16) a 2025 priority.

q_prop_tax_eliminate.summary: Says Texas is on a path to eliminate school property taxes for every homeowner within two or three sessions through larger homestead exemptions, but argues eliminating property taxes entirely would lead to massive sales tax increases.

q_medicaid.summary: Said in 2025, "We are one of the states that did not go along with that Medicaid expansion and thank goodness," and in 2018 called not expanding Medicaid one of the best things the Senate did.

q_gambling.summary: Has kept casino and sports betting amendments from reaching a Senate vote, citing a lack of support among Senate Republicans; he has not publicly stated a personal view on letting voters decide.

q_trans_minors.summary: Called gender transition treatment for minors abhorrent and made SB 14 (2023), which bans it, one of his top priorities.

issue_notes.summary: Made raising the homestead exemption to $140,000, and to $200,000 for seniors, top 2025 priorities, along with business tax relief.
Designated bills on a parental bill of rights and limiting inappropriate books in schools as 2025 priorities.
Designated a Texas DOGE government efficiency bill as a 2025 priority.

candidates.name: Vikki Goodwin
candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 47 (Travis County), since 2019; Democratic nominee for lieutenant governor
candidates.background: Vikki Goodwin runs a residential real estate business with her husband and has represented parts of Austin and the Lake Travis area in the Texas House since 2019. She grew up in Dallas and holds a business degree from the University of Texas at Austin and a master's degree from the LBJ School of Public Affairs. In the 2025 session she served on the Appropriations and Insurance committees. She won the Democratic nomination in a May 26, 2026 runoff with 67.8 percent.

priorities.text: Campaigns on well-funded neighborhood public schools and opposes vouchers.
Campaigns on protecting water and putting families ahead of data centers.
Campaigns on comprehensive, affordable health care through her Texas Cares plan.
Campaigns on affordable housing, including limiting tax increases and keeping rents down.
Says the Senate needs a leader who solicits ideas from the entire body.

promises.text: Proposes a three-tier Texas Cares plan: Medicaid expansion up to 138 percent of the poverty level, a state Basic Health Program for incomes up to 200 percent, and a state-run insurance option for all Texans.
Pledges as lieutenant governor to prioritize bills regulating data centers, making them pay for their electricity and water and giving counties power to regulate them.
Calls for a pause on new data center construction until comprehensive legislation passes.
Says she will pursue a regulatory framework for THC with age limits, testing and labeling instead of prohibition.
Supports raising the minimum wage to at least $15 an hour.

record.text: Passed Cati's Act (2023) on drowning prevention at child care facilities and the Natalia Cox Act (2023) providing resources to domestic violence victims.
Filed a 2023 bill for universal background checks and a three-day waiting period for gun purchases; it died in committee.
Voted against SB 2 (2025), the education savings account program, and for HB 2 (2025), the school finance bill.
Voted against SB 8 (2021), the six-week abortion ban, HB 1927 (2021), permitless carry, and SB 1 (2021), the election law.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), the bail bill, and SJR 5 (2025), the bail constitutional amendment.
Voted for HJR 7 (2025), the dedicated water fund amendment, and SB 7 (2025), on water infrastructure financing.
Voted for HB 441 (2021) and HB 218 (2023), reducing penalties for marijuana possession, and for HB 46 (2025), expanding the Compassionate Use Program; was recorded absent on SB 3 (2025), the THC ban.
Voted against HB 2127 (2023), the preemption law, HB 1243 (2023), the illegal voting penalty increase, and SB 2627 (2023), the electric generation funding bill.
Voted against the House versions of the 2023 and 2025 state budgets.
Took part in the 2025 quorum break over congressional redistricting and voted against HB 4 (2025), the new map.
Voted for HB 2730 in 2021, which regulated land acquisition by entities with eminent domain authority; it passed the House 143 to 1.

notes.text: Attorney General Ken Paxton sought to remove Goodwin and 12 other House Democrats from office over the 2025 quorum break; the Texas Supreme Court dismissed the case in May 2026.
In September 2026 she filed a police complaint alleging that two AI-generated ads by the Patrick campaign violated the state deepfake law; the ads were removed the next day.
Endorsed by EMILYs List and by the editorial boards of the Austin American-Statesman, Houston Chronicle and San Antonio Express-News.
Says she holds an A+ rating from Equality Texas.
A poll of likely voters in late July 2026 found 56 percent of respondents did not know enough about Goodwin to have an opinion.

q_prop_tax_eliminate.summary: Supports property tax relief through the state taking greater responsibility for funding education and other services, but does not propose eliminating school property taxes.

q_min_wage.summary: Supports raising the minimum wage to at least $15 an hour and raising the tipped-worker wage.

q_vouchers.summary: Has voted against vouchers, including SB 2 (2025), and calls the program a terrible deal for Texas kids.

q_school_funding.summary: Wants to raise the basic allotment to previous levels, keep funding in line with inflation and raise teacher pay.

q_ten_commandments.summary: Voted against SB 10 (2025) and says public money should not fund religious education.

q_medicaid.summary: Proposes Medicaid expansion as the first tier of her Texas Cares plan.

q_abortion.summary: Calls for restoring full reproductive care and voted against the 2021 six-week ban.

q_border_state.summary: Supports comprehensive federal immigration reform and says Texas does not have to keep buying into the current approach; voted against SB 4 (2023).

q_deportation.summary: Criticizes what she calls ruthless and often illegal detention of people who call Texas home and voted against SB 8 (2025).

q_legal_status.summary: Supports comprehensive immigration reform and cites uncertainty for DACA students and refugees.

q_gun_laws.summary: Supports stronger background checks, training requirements and tools against straw purchases, and filed a universal background check bill in 2023.

q_bail.summary: Voted for SB 9 (2025) and SJR 5 (2025), expanding the denial of bail in certain cases.

q_cannabis.summary: Supports regulating THC rather than prohibiting it and proposes funding part of her health plan with a tax on legal cannabis.

q_fossil_priority.summary: Voted against SB 2627 (2023), which created funding mechanisms for new electric generating facilities.

q_water.summary: Voted for the 2025 water fund amendment and water financing bill, while saying conservation and reuse should be part of the answer and drinking water should come before data centers.

q_voting_access.summary: Supports online voter registration, expanded voting options and ranked choice voting in local elections.

q_election_fraud.summary: Voted against HB 1243 (2023), which increased the criminal penalty for illegal voting.

q_preemption.summary: Voted against HB 2127 (2023), which limits local ordinances.

q_gambling.summary: Favors letting Texas voters decide whether to legalize gambling.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted against SB 14 (2023), the state ban on gender transition treatments for minors.

q_foreign_land.summary: Voted against SB 17 (2025) restricting land purchases by certain foreign entities.

q_eminent_domain.summary: Voted for HB 2730 (2021), which added rules for land acquisition by entities with eminent domain authority; the bill passed the House nearly unanimously.

issue_notes.summary: Supports a constitutional amendment allowing citizen-initiated statewide ballot measures (HJR 198).
Proposes the Fair Rent Incentive Act lowering the appraisal cap for landlords who charge fair market rent or less, and automatic homestead exemptions at closing.
Supports an employer contribution to fund child care and expanding Pre-K eligibility to children of public school employees.
Wants laws putting people and animals first for water, studies before construction and penalties for companies that do not report water use.

candidates.name: Mayes Middleton
candidates.current_role: Texas state senator, District 11, since 2023; president of Middleton Oil Company
candidates.background: Mayes Middleton is a Galveston-area oil and gas executive, rancher and attorney who earned his law degree from the University of Texas School of Law in 2008. He served two terms in the Texas House, where he chaired the House Freedom Caucus, before winning a state Senate seat in 2022. He won the Republican nomination for attorney general by defeating U.S. Rep. Chip Roy in the May 26, 2026 runoff with about 56 percent of the vote.

priorities.text: Campaigns on backing President Trump's border security agenda and deportation orders, including suing cities that he says violate the state ban on sanctuary policies.
Campaigns on election integrity, including enforcement of Texas voter ID laws so that only qualified U.S. citizens vote.
Campaigns on zero tolerance for violent crime and on reining in district attorneys he says refuse to enforce state law.
Campaigns on keeping transgender women out of women's restrooms, locker rooms and sports.
Campaigns on open records enforcement and a "DOGE Texas" approach to waste and fraud in government spending.
Says he will protect oil and gas jobs and Texas energy independence.

promises.text: Says he will create a standalone election integrity division in the attorney general's office with law enforcement powers.
Says he will sue local officials who obstruct federal immigration enforcement and seek civil and criminal penalties and removal from office.
Says he will seek stronger bonds for dangerous offenders and increased consequences for district attorneys who do not enforce state law.
Says he will sue corporations for deceptive trade practices and oppose foreign adversaries buying Texas assets.

record.text: Authored Senate Bill 8 (2025), which requires people in public schools, universities and government buildings to use restrooms matching their sex at birth; Gov. Abbott signed it in September 2025.
Sponsored and passed the Save Women's Sports Act, which bars transgender women from competing in women's collegiate sports.
Sponsored a 2025 bill allowing schools to set aside class time for prayer and Bible reading.
Passed legislation allowing the attorney general's office to take election fraud cases without waiting for a local prosecutor, according to a candidate profile.
Voted with the Senate majority for Senate Bill 2 (2025), which created the state's education savings account program; all Senate Democrats and one Republican opposed it.
Voted to acquit Attorney General Ken Paxton at his 2023 impeachment trial; the Tribune reported he had been among senators considering a vote to convict.
In 2025 sponsored a bill to limit offshore wind projects, and in 2022 wrote to the Biden administration opposing a proposed wind farm off the Galveston coast.
Cosponsored a bill by Sen. Nathan Johnson strengthening consumer protections for commercial genetic testing.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned hemp-derived THC products; Gov. Abbott vetoed it.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), which bars gender transition treatments for minors.
As a House member, voted for SB 1 (2021), the election law that added voting rules and criminal penalties.
As a House member, voted for HB 2730 (2021), which regulated land acquisition by entities with eminent domain authority; it passed 143 to 1.

notes.text: Put more than $16 million of his own money into the primary and runoff, according to the Tribune in May 2026; later Tribune reporting put his self-funding above $20 million.

Over about 15 years he donated millions to conservative candidates and groups, including most initial members of the House Freedom Caucus, and was the main funder of Matt Krause's 2022 primary challenge to Ken Paxton. Chip Roy accused him of buying endorsements; Middleton did not respond to that request for comment.
Ran ads calling himself "MAGA Mayes" and told NBC DFW, "I am 100% pro-Trump." Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick endorsed him in the runoff.
Critics, including his runoff opponent, noted he has practiced law only for his family company and has little courtroom experience.
Did not respond to the League of Women Voters of Texas questionnaire for its November 2026 voters guide.

priorities.text: Campaigns on returning the attorney general's office to core duties such as child support collection, legal opinions, public finance review and open government.
Campaigns on enforcing consumer protection and antitrust laws against price gouging, junk fees, scams and unfair competition.
Campaigns on investigating and prosecuting public corruption "irrespective of political party."
Campaigns on an office independent of both political parties and of any presidential administration.
Campaigns on public safety through partnership with district attorneys and the office's own authority over identity theft, cybercrime, Medicaid fraud and some human trafficking cases.

promises.text: Says he will make improving the child support division a priority, citing complaints about delays and service.
Says he will join other states in suing the Trump administration over actions he considers illegal, while saying he will not sue "for fun."
Says he will produce recommendations to the Legislature on how consumer protection, competition and employment laws apply to artificial intelligence within his first 30 days.
Says he will not defend the Ten Commandments classroom display law while appeals continue and will not devote resources to enforcing Senate Bill 8, the 2025 restroom law.
Says he will audit Deloitte and other state vendors after the Department of Public Safety failed to transmit more than 150,000 voter registration applications.
Says he will review actions taken under Ken Paxton and support House Democrats' litigation against the 2025 mid-decade redistricting plan.

record.text: Voted to convict Ken Paxton at his 2023 impeachment trial, as part of the Senate minority.
Voted against Senate Bill 2 in 2025, which created the education savings account program; all Senate Democrats opposed it.
Filed bills as a senator to restore abortion access and to expand Medicaid.
Authored a bill strengthening consumer protections for commercial genetic testing, which Mayes Middleton cosponsored.
Voted for Senate Bill 2972 (2025), a campus protest law, which he noted drew bipartisan support.

Says his legislative work secured $2 billion for backup power at water plants, nursing homes and first responder facilities, and updated state law on data privacy, artificial intelligence and cybersecurity.

Voted for SB 3 (2025), the hemp-derived THC ban, while stating in the Senate Journal that an outright ban is not the right approach and that he favors decriminalizing small amounts and a legal, regulated THC market; Gov. Abbott later vetoed the bill.
Filed SB 2028 (2025) to decriminalize marijuana possession and reduce sentencing ranges, and SB 928 (2025) to add chronic pain to the Compassionate Use Program, according to his reason for vote.
Voted against SB 17 (2025), which restricts land purchases by people and entities tied to certain foreign nations.
Voted against SB 14 (2023), which bars gender transition treatments for minors.
Voted for SB 9 and SJR 5 (2025), expanding the denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted against SB 1 (2021), the election law that added voting rules and criminal penalties.

notes.text: Endorsed by the Texas AFL-CIO, Sierra Club, Everytown for Gun Safety and the Texas Federation of Teachers, according to his campaign site.

Former Republican state Sen. John Carona, a past supporter of the Texas Tribune, is one of his larger donors, according to the Tribune's disclosure.

candidates.background: Don Huffines is a Dallas real estate developer who co-founded Huffines Communities and holds a business degree from the University of Texas at Austin. priorities.text: Campaigns on auditing government spending, which he calls "DOGE-ing Texas," and returning savings to taxpayers as property tax relief.
Campaigns on reducing and ultimately eliminating property taxes, saying Texans should not spend their lives "paying perpetual rent through property taxes."
Campaigns on implementing and promoting the state's education savings account program.
Campaigns on reducing regulations he says raise housing and business costs, and on favoring Texas-based companies in state contracting.

promises.text: Pledged not to take a state salary, and declined it as his first official act.
Says he will audit state spending and highway construction contracts.
Says he will prioritize marketing the $1 billion education savings account program so parents know it exists.
Says he will work with state leaders on property tax relief in the next legislative session.

record.text: Ordered a performance review of the comptroller's office in August 2026, citing a directive from state leaders to cut agency spending by 3 percent.
In August 2026 urged cities and counties to lower property tax rates because of rising sales tax collections, and announced performance reviews of school district spending.
As a state senator, led the effort to abolish the Dallas County Schools bus agency after uncovering financial problems that led to a federal bribery investigation.
Authored a property tax exemption for surviving spouses of first responders killed in the line of duty.
Filed a bill as a senator to study the cost of a private school voucher program; it did not pass.

notes.text: Gov. Abbott appointed him comptroller on July 2, 2026, after acting Comptroller Kelly Hancock resigned; Sarah Eckhardt called the appointment a way to install a loyalist before voters decide.
Largely self-funded his primary campaign and reported $11.7 million cash on hand in January 2026; endorsed by U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz.
Founded the Huffines Liberty Foundation after leaving the Senate.

candidates.name: Dawn Buckingham
candidates.current_role: Texas Land Commissioner since January 2023
candidates.background: Dawn Buckingham is an oculoplastic surgeon with a bachelor's degree from the University of Texas at Austin and a medical degree from the University of Texas Medical Branch. She served on the Lake Travis ISD board and represented Senate District 24 from 2017 to 2023. She became the first woman to lead the General Land Office in 2023 and was unopposed in the 2026 Republican primary.

priorities.text: Campaigns on border security, which she calls a pillar of her campaign, including use of state land for border barriers and immigration enforcement.
Campaigns on protecting the oil and gas industry, which she links to national security, and on developing geothermal, nuclear and natural gas power on state lands.
Campaigns on growing Permanent School Fund contributions to public education.
Campaigns on serving veterans through the Veterans Land Board, veterans homes and cemeteries.
Campaigns on disaster recovery and flood mitigation funding.
Campaigns on restoring the Alamo and protecting Texas history from what she calls "revision."

promises.text: Says she will complete a new Alamo visitor center and museum.
Says the Alamo Cenotaph "will never be moved."
Says she will protect 2.5 million oil and gas jobs.

record.text: Launched the Jocelyn Initiative to commit General Land Office resources to detaining and deporting people in the country illegally, and in November 2024 pledged state land to support federal deportation efforts.
Declared Rio Grande islands Texas territory to give the Department of Public Safety operational control, and bought riverfront property for a border wall right-of-way, according to her campaign.
Ordered federal contractors to stop clearing a state border tract near Big Bend after a lawsuit from Presidio leaders.
Says her office has delivered over $9 billion in disaster recovery, $1 billion in flood mitigation and nearly $6 billion for public education; these are campaign figures.
Sued the Biden administration over endangered species listings and efforts to halt liquefied natural gas exports, according to her campaign.
As a state senator, filed a bill to impose civil penalties on faithless presidential electors.
As a state senator, voted with the full Senate for HB 2730 (2021), which regulated land acquisition by entities with eminent domain authority and right-of-way agents.

notes.text: Former Alamo Trust CEO Kate Rogers left in October 2025 after Buckingham criticized an Indigenous Peoples' Day post as "woke"; Rogers sued Buckingham and others, and in August 2026 a federal judge allowed most claims, including a First Amendment claim against Buckingham, to proceed.
Endorsed by President Trump, House Speaker Dustin Burrows, the National Border Patrol Council and the Texas Oil and Gas Association; reported about $3.2 million cash on hand on June 30, 2026.
In 2023 she relayed a Texas A&M professor's lecture remarks criticizing Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick; the professor was investigated and cleared about two weeks later.

q_border_state.summary: Has used General Land Office land and resources for border barriers and immigration enforcement.

q_fossil_priority.summary: Emphasizes oil, gas, geothermal and nuclear power on state lands; no statement on wind or solar was found.

q_deportation.summary: Created the Jocelyn Initiative to offer state resources for detention and deportation and pledged state land for federal deportation efforts.

q_eminent_domain.summary: Voted with the full Senate for HB 2730 (2021), which added rules for land acquisition by entities with eminent domain authority.

issue_notes.summary: Says she wants Texas to lead on reuse of produced water from oil and gas operations.
Has opposed recognizing Indigenous history at the Alamo in the way the former Alamo Trust leadership proposed.

candidates.name: Jon Rosenthal
candidates.current_role: Texas state representative, District 135 (northwest Houston), since 2019
candidates.background: Jon Rosenthal is an oil field mechanical engineer with more than 20 years in and around the oil and gas industry as an engineer, project manager and team leader. He has represented House District 135, around Cypress, since 2019 and is serving his fourth term. He was unopposed in the 2026 Democratic primary and did not seek reelection to the House.

priorities.text: Campaigns on enforcing existing commission rules and barring new permits for companies that violate them.
Campaigns on ending routine flaring and venting of natural gas except in emergencies, with leak detection requirements and help for small operators.
Campaigns on fair, predictable gas utility rates, opposing junk fees and charges for preventable storm failures.
Campaigns on a more accessible commission with regional liaisons, evening hearings and language access.
Calls himself a "drill, baby, drill" Democrat who supports an "all of the above" energy strategy.

promises.text: Says he will require gas capture with enforceable timelines, supported by compliance clinics for small operators.
Says he will expand well plugging, seek more industry funding for it and publish public dashboards.
Says he will apply stricter prudence reviews before utilities recover extraordinary costs and require plain-language bills.
Says he will set up a 24/7 complaint hotline with case tracking and neighborhood air monitoring pilots.
Says he will strengthen enforcement of natural gas weatherization requirements.
Says data centers should file water and power resource plans before construction and should not be built next to homes.
Proposes funding the plugging of abandoned wells with a new fee on saltwater disposal and higher operator bonds and cash deposits.
Says he will lobby for heavier fines and bonding for bad operators, third-party audits and site-level compliance reporting.

record.text: Has served in the Texas House since 2019, representing a northwest Houston district.

Filed bills in 2021 (HB 1452) and 2023 (HB 1459) directing the Railroad Commission to adopt a policy to eliminate routine flaring of natural gas; both were referred to the Energy Resources Committee and did not advance.

Filed bills in 2021 (HB 3182), 2023 (HB 3181) and 2025 (HB 575) on weather emergency preparedness for natural gas facilities, the later versions increasing civil and administrative penalties; none advanced past committee referral.

Filed HB 3480 in 2019 to require disclosure of the composition of fluids carried by pipelines regulated by the Railroad Commission, and HB 2745 in 2021 on commission regulation of carbon dioxide storage.
Filed HB 5106 in 2025 on information that payers of oil and gas proceeds must give royalty owners; it was left pending in committee.
Voted for SB 2627 in 2023, which created funding mechanisms for new electric generating facilities (the Texas Energy Fund), and was a joint author of HB 4584 in 2025 on the same subject.
Voted for HB 2730 in 2021, which regulated land acquisition by entities with eminent domain authority and right-of-way agents; it passed the House 143 to 1.

notes.text: Endorsed by the Sierra Club, Texas AFL-CIO, the Houston Chronicle and Austin American-Statesman editorial boards, and former GOP Railroad Commission candidate Hawk Dunlap; Republican strategist Karl Rove said he would vote for him.
Outraised French in the third quarter of 2026, with about $488,000; neither candidate received money from major oil and gas industry PACs in that period.
French's campaign linked Rosenthal to the Bolshevik Revolution, a claim the Forward criticized as antisemitic.

Says he would never shut down an energy source until a replacement exists and that oil and gas is not going anywhere soon.

candidates.current_role: Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Texas since January 2025; justice since 2018
candidates.background: Blacklock was born in Houston and grew up in Missouri City. He holds a bachelor's degree from the University of Texas at Austin and a law degree from Yale Law School, and clerked for Judge Jerry Smith of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. He worked in the Texas Attorney General's Office under Greg Abbott, later serving as deputy attorney general, and was Gov. Abbott's general counsel from 2015 to 2018. Abbott appointed him to the court in 2018 and named him chief justice in 2025.

priorities.text: Campaigns on the themes "Keep Texas Strong. Keep Texans Free. Defend the Constitution."
Describes the judge's role as a "neutral arbiter of the law" who applies the law "fairly, equally, and according to its original meaning."
As chief justice, asked the Legislature in 2025 to raise district judges' base pay by 30 percent, saying Texas ranked 48th of 50 states in district judge pay.
Proposed lowering the cost of legal services, including by allowing qualified non-lawyers to provide some basic legal services.
Said the State Bar of Texas must "remain completely politically neutral."
Says he has tried to foster a collegial culture on the court in which justices respect each other's opinions and work together on difficult cases.

record.text: Wrote the 2026 majority opinion declining Gov. Abbott's request to remove state Rep. Gene Wu from office over the 2025 quorum break, writing that courts have recognized it is not their role to resolve disputes between the other two branches.

Wrote the 2022 opinion in In re Abbott that lifted a statewide injunction against state child-abuse investigations of parents of transgender youth while holding that the governor lacked authority to direct such investigations.
Wrote a 2024 concurrence in State v. Loe, in which the court upheld Texas' ban on gender-transition medical treatment for minors.
Wrote the 2023 majority opinion in Abbott v. Harris County holding that local officials could not impose COVID-19 orders more restrictive than the governor's.
Wrote a 2020 concurrence in In re Salon A La Mode questioning the constitutionality of some COVID-19 government orders.
Wrote a 2021 opinion holding that the Texas Constitution allows each legislative chamber to compel the attendance of absent members.

In his 2025 State of the Judiciary address, asked the court's advisory committee to propose ending rotating (central) dockets and to study deferring merits briefing until after a petition for review is granted.

Joined Justice Kyle Hawkins' dissent, except as to one part, in State v. JRJ Pusok Holdings and joined Hawkins' concurrence in the judgment in River Creek Development Corp. v. Preston Hollow Capital (June 2026).

Cited his 2024 position upholding the State Fair of Texas ban on guns, which Attorney General Ken Paxton opposed, as an example of ruling against Republican leaders, according to The Dallas Morning News.
Wrote the court's unanimous 2019 opinion in Burlington Resources Oil and Gas v. Texas Crude Energy, which he calls one of his most challenging cases.

Wrote a 2024 concurrence, joined by Justice Devine, in Hensley v. State Commission on Judicial Conduct, saying the court should have gone beyond its ruling that the judge's lawsuit could largely proceed and held that the commission lacks authority to sanction a judge who declines, for religious reasons, to perform same-sex weddings while referring couples to another officiant.

notes.text: In the State Bar of Texas 2026 judicial poll, a nonbinding attorney preference poll taken before the March primary, Blacklock received 1,678 votes, Maggie Ellis 1,259 and Cory Carlyle 894. The bar states the poll is not an endorsement.
Endorsed by Gov. Greg Abbott, Texas Alliance for Life, Texas Right to Life and the Texas Civil Justice League; Ballotpedia also lists Texas Values Action and True Texas Project.
Reported $783,574 cash on hand as of June 30, 2026; top donors included Texans for Lawsuit Reform PAC ($25,000) and Hunton Andrews Kurth PAC ($15,000).
Before joining the court, he worked on litigation defending Texas abortion laws and challenging the Affordable Care Act, according to the Texas Tribune.

In 2025 he told the State Bar of Texas to remain politically neutral; Bloomberg Law reported this followed bar disciplinary cases against Attorney General Ken Paxton and others over the 2020 election, which the defendants won.
Won his 2024 re-election with 58.3 percent of the vote; The Dallas Morning News editorial board recommended him that year.
Unopposed in the March 2026 Republican primary.

The Dallas Morning News editorial board recommended Blacklock in the general election, citing his experience and his work on judicial pay and on the use of artificial intelligence in courts, while writing that both candidates had displayed behavior it considered too partisan.
Spoke at the Texas Republican Party convention in summer 2026 and told The Dallas Morning News he rejects the claim that his opinions are influenced by Gov. Abbott or Republican leaders.
Lists his roles as chairman of the Texas Judicial Council and member of the Texas Indigent Defense Commission, and as a former member of the Access to Justice Commission.

q_textualism.summary: Describes himself as an originalist and said in 2025 that the Constitution "means the same thing yesterday, today, and tomorrow" until the people change it.

q_judicial_selection.summary: Wrote that no selection system is perfect but that elections let the people control their constitution by changing the court's membership, while acknowledging that judicial fundraising invites suspicion of conflicts.

issue_notes.summary: In 2025 he supported the governor's priority to let judges keep defendants accused of violent crimes in custody before trial, which required a constitutional amendment.
Urged repeal of a Family Code provision allowing termination of parental rights for failing to complete a service plan, and said removing children should be a last resort.
Disagrees that the court is slanted toward business, writing that the court applies statutes the Legislature enacted as written, including ones some call pro-business, rather than resisting them.
Supports reasonable contribution limits and full disclosure, says donors receive nothing in return, and says the state should remain open to reforms that address the perception of influence.

candidates.name: Maggie Ellis
candidates.current_role: Justice, Texas Third Court of Appeals (Austin) since January 2025
candidates.background: Ellis lives in Georgetown. She holds an associate's degree from Austin Community College, a bachelor's degree from the University of Texas at Austin and a law degree from Baylor Law School. She has worked as a public school teacher, a Travis County assistant district attorney, an administrative law judge at the State Office of Administrative Hearings, and a private attorney in juvenile and family law, and is board certified in juvenile law. She was elected to the Third Court of Appeals in 2024 after an unsuccessful 2020 run for the 200th District Court.

priorities.text: Campaigns on removing politics from the judiciary and expanding access to justice.
Says her guiding principle is "you can't serve people you don't see."
Emphasizes efficiency, thorough preparation and responsible case management, and supports accessible and responsive appellate courts.
Says she prioritizes fairness, due process and equal treatment under the law.
Said she is running in part out of concern about what she sees as politicization of the Supreme Court, noting that Gov. Abbott appointed seven of its nine justices.
Says the chief justice role requires administering all Texas courts and cites her experience leading large organizations and as in-house counsel for a government department.

record.text: Sat on the Third Court of Appeals panel, with Justices Gisela Triana and Chari Kelly, that upheld about $181,000 in sanctions against developer Nate Paul, according to Kelly's campaign summary of Law360 coverage.

notes.text: Said she decided to run after the Supreme Court issued guidance that judges need not perform same-sex weddings, which she called "an attack on our community and our Constitution."
Won the March 2026 Democratic primary over former Fifth Court of Appeals Justice Cory Carlyle with about 77 percent of the vote.
In the State Bar of Texas 2026 judicial poll, taken before the primary, Ellis received 1,259 votes, Jimmy Blacklock 1,678 and Cory Carlyle 894. The bar states the poll is not an endorsement.

Endorsed by the Texas AFL-CIO, Stonewall Democrats of Austin, The Caucus, Bexar County Young Democrats and other Democratic groups; Wikipedia and Ballotpedia list EMILYs List and the Houston Chronicle editorial board.
The Dallas Morning News editorial board recommended Carlyle over Ellis in the Democratic primary, citing his longer appellate judicial experience.
Reported $53,034 cash on hand as of June 30, 2026, after raising $33,766 from January through June.

The Dallas Morning News editorial board recommended Blacklock in the general election and wrote that Ellis was too progressive in her interview; she told the board the Supreme Court is too far right and "is no longer independent."

The San Antonio Express-News recommended her in the March Democratic primary, citing her vision for the court; the Houston Chronicle also recommended her in the primary, citing her administrative experience.
Received the Hays County Bar Association Pro Bono Hero award and is a former chair of the State Bar of Texas Juvenile Law Section.

q_textualism.summary: Did not adopt the textualist label, writing that courts should follow precedent in most cases but that laws should allow flexibility to shift with changes in values, though not with political pressure.

q_judicial_selection.summary: Wrote that Texas should not move to appointing Supreme Court justices because elections can inspire confidence in courts and let voters remove judges, while noting campaign costs and one-party dominance as weaknesses.

issue_notes.summary: Agrees that the court's case selection and outcomes tend to favor businesses and that it is slanted against civil plaintiffs.

Told the Express-News she is concerned about the court dropping the requirement that law schools be accredited by the American Bar Association and that the court should focus on indigent defense and legal access.

Supports more concrete guidance under the Code of Judicial Conduct, judicial mentorship and training programs, and review of whether recent changes to selecting the review tribunal provide enough independence.

candidates.name: James P. Sullivan
candidates.current_role: Justice, Supreme Court of Texas, Place 2, since January 2025 (appointed)
candidates.background: Sullivan was raised in Austin and graduated from Rice University and Harvard Law School, where he was an editor of the Harvard Law Review. He clerked for Judge Thomas B. Griffith of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, served as an assistant solicitor general under then-Attorney General Greg Abbott, practiced as an appellate litigator and taught as an adjunct professor. He was Gov. Abbott's deputy general counsel and then general counsel before Abbott appointed him to the court in January 2025; it is his first judgeship.

priorities.text: Campaigns on "bold, relentless, conservative judging."
Says he will "run through a wall for the rule of law."
Says the court needs judges who "won't back down when our freedoms are on the line."

record.text: Wrote a concurrence in the 2026 Gene Wu quorum-break case stating that if lawmakers broke quorum again, "the next set of quorumbreakers had better be ready to pay us a visit."
Joined Justice Kyle Hawkins' dissent in State v. JRJ Pusok Holdings and joined Justice Busby's majority opinion in River Creek Development Corp. v. Preston Hollow Capital (June 2026).
His opinions are noted for frequent footnotes and references to fictional characters, including in In re State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co. and American Midstream v. Rainbow Energy Marketing.

Wrote a solo 2025 dissent in Perez v. City of San Antonio arguing the court should have declined to answer the Fifth Circuit's certified question about the Texas Constitution's protection of religious services.

Wrote the court's October 2025 opinion in Gonzalez v. Texas Medical Board allowing a former congressional candidate, who holds a medical degree but no medical license, to proceed with claims challenging the board's cease-and-desist order over his campaign use of the titles "Dr." and "physician", without deciding the merits.

notes.text: In the State Bar of Texas 2026 judicial poll, taken before the primary, Sullivan received 1,508 votes and Chari Kelly 2,112. The bar states the poll is not an endorsement.
Endorsed by Gov. Greg Abbott, Texas Alliance for Life and the Texas Civil Justice League.
Reported $590,381 cash on hand as of June 30, 2026; top donors included Texans for Lawsuit Reform PAC ($25,000) and Jackson Walker PAC ($15,000).
In 2012 a federal appeals judge criticized a rehearing petition he filed as "disturbingly unprofessional," according to the Texas Tribune and The Dallas Morning News.
The Texas Tribune reported that he has sought a federal judgeship in Austin.
The Dallas Morning News editorial board recommended Chari Kelly in the general election, citing her longer judicial experience and criticizing his Wu concurrence and the 2012 petition.
Unopposed in the March 2026 Republican primary.
Asked in the Dallas Morning News primary questionnaire whether Texas should move to appointing justices, he declined to give a view and referred to Articles V and XVII of the Texas Constitution.

q_textualism.summary: Calls himself a textualist whose analysis begins and often ends with the governing text, and says an issue resolved by the original public meaning of that text ends the inquiry.

issue_notes.summary: Disagrees that the court is pro-business, saying each decision rests on the facts and the law without regard to the parties' names.

candidates.name: Chari Kelly
candidates.current_role: Justice, Texas Third Court of Appeals (Austin), Place 3, since 2019
candidates.background: Kelly lives in Austin. She earned a bachelor's degree from the University of Florida and a law degree from the University of Texas, then served in the U.S. Army from 2003 to 2007 as a Judge Advocate General's Corps captain and paratrooper. She was a research attorney at the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals, an assistant attorney general in the Medicaid fraud unit, and a felony prosecutor in Comal and Travis counties before joining the Third Court of Appeals. She is board certified in judicial administration and criminal law and teaches trial advocacy at the University of Texas School of Law.

priorities.text: Says Texans deserve a Supreme Court with judges who have "real courtroom experience, appellate experience, independence, balance, and respect for the Constitution."
Campaigns on experience, citing eight years on the Third Court of Appeals and more than 800 authored opinions.
Campaigns on judicial independence, saying the law applies to everyone, including those in power.
Campaigns on public confidence in courts that apply the law consistently and put "justice over politics."
Says she is personally passionate about fair courts, access to justice, civil legal aid and public confidence in the judiciary.
Says the Supreme Court has become "a rubber stamp for the executive branch" and that she is running to bring balance and independence.

promises.text: Says she will bring the same independence, discipline and respect for the Constitution she showed on the Third Court of Appeals to the Supreme Court.

record.text: Says she ruled on the Third Court of Appeals that the Texas attorney general was not above the law in a whistleblower case.
Says she ruled that the governor does not possess absolute authority under the Texas Disaster Act.
Has ruled on cases involving public health, environmental issues and criminal justice on the Third Court of Appeals since 2019.

Dissented from a 2-1 Third Court of Appeals ruling upholding state permits for industrial waste injection wells in Montgomery County, writing that the majority disregarded findings of two administrative law judges.

notes.text: In the State Bar of Texas 2026 judicial poll, taken before the primary, Kelly received 2,112 votes and James P. Sullivan 1,508. Kelly says this was the highest total of any candidate in the ten contested statewide judicial races. The bar states the poll is not an endorsement.

Reports endorsements from the Houston Lawyers Association, Mexican American Bar Association of Houston, Hispanic Bar Association of Austin and Austin Black Lawyers Association, as well as EMILY's List and the Texas AFL-CIO.
The Dallas Morning News editorial board recommended Kelly for Place 2.
Former Austin Bar president; named Travis County prosecutor of the year by Mothers Against Drunk Driving in 2018.
Reported $105,425 cash on hand as of June 30, 2026, after raising $57,056 from January through June.
Unopposed in the March 2026 Democratic primary.

q_textualism.summary: Says she does not adopt the textualist or constructionist labels and describes her approach as pragmatic, considering text and precedent without ignoring changed circumstances, while saying judges should not rewrite statutes.

q_judicial_selection.summary: Wrote that neither system is ideal but Texas should keep electing judges because elections give voters a direct voice and appointments give the executive branch too much influence.

issue_notes.summary: Agrees the court is seen as pro-business and says every case seeking discretionary review should get equal consideration regardless of the parties' wealth or power.
Supports strong disclosure, clear recusal standards, timely handling of misconduct complaints and more transparency and resources for the State Commission on Judicial Conduct.

candidates.name: Kyle Hawkins
candidates.current_role: Justice, Supreme Court of Texas, Place 7, since October 2025 (appointed)
candidates.background: Hawkins lives in Austin. He holds a bachelor's degree from Harvard College and a law degree from the University of Minnesota Law School, and clerked for Justice Samuel Alito of the U.S. Supreme Court and Judge Edith Jones of the Fifth Circuit. He was Texas solicitor general from 2018 to 2021, a partner at Gibson Dunn and Crutcher, Counselor to the U.S. Solicitor General, and chair of the Texas appellate practice at Lehotsky Keller Cohn. Gov. Abbott appointed him in October 2025 to succeed retiring Justice Jeff Boyd.

priorities.text: Says the court's work "demands humility, diligence, and a commitment to applying the law as written."
Cites respect for the U.S. and Texas constitutions and the rule of law as guiding his career.
Told Bloomberg Law his job is to "uphold the rule of law by applying the law as written without fear or favor."

record.text: Wrote a dissent, joined by Justice Sullivan and in part by Chief Justice Blacklock, in State v. JRJ Pusok Holdings (June 2026).
Wrote an opinion concurring in the judgment, joined by Chief Justice Blacklock, in River Creek Development Corp. v. Preston Hollow Capital (June 2026).

As Texas solicitor general and in private practice, litigated against the Affordable Care Act and Planned Parenthood and defended Texas election laws; he has also testified to Congress on constitutional issues with the Voting Rights Act.
Has argued five cases before the U.S. Supreme Court and nine before the Texas Supreme Court.

Wrote the court's June 2026 opinion in In re K.N., which affirmed termination of a mother's parental rights but held the evidence legally insufficient to support the endangerment findings against the father and sent his case back to the court of appeals, stating that a termination order "must always be a last resort and never a first impulse."

notes.text: In the State Bar of Texas 2026 judicial poll, taken before the primary, Kyle Hawkins received 1,203 votes, Kristen Hawkins 1,705 and Gordon Goodman 674. The bar states the poll is not an endorsement.
Endorsed by Gov. Greg Abbott and the Texas Civil Justice League.
Reported $216,374 cash on hand as of June 30, 2026; top donors included Texans for Lawsuit Reform PAC ($25,000) and Bracewell PAC ($10,000).

KERA reported that he resigned as solicitor general shortly after not signing onto the 2020 lawsuit asking the U.S. Supreme Court to overturn the presidential election results; the attorney general's office gave no reason for the resignation.
Served about three months in 2025 on the U.S. Justice Department transition team for the Office of the Solicitor General.
Weeks before his appointment he argued before the Texas Supreme Court as an advocate in a case over the taxation of nicotine pouches.
Did not complete The Dallas Morning News Voter Guide or interview; the editorial board recommended Kristen Hawkins.
Unopposed in the March 2026 Republican primary.

q_textualism.summary: Says judges should apply "the law as written" without fear or favor, though he has not detailed a broader interpretive theory in sources found.

candidates.name: Kristen Hawkins
candidates.current_role: Judge, 11th District Court (Harris County) since 2017
candidates.background: Hawkins grew up in Houston and attended Alief Hastings High School. She holds a bachelor's degree in government and Spanish from the University of Texas at Austin and a law degree with honors from South Texas College of Law Houston. Before taking the bench she practiced civil litigation, including Social Security disability claims, and served as a Harris County tax master. She was elected to the 11th District Court in 2016 and re-elected in 2020.

priorities.text: Campaigns on her trial-court experience, arguing the Supreme Court would benefit from the perspective of district judges who implement its rulings.
Says the Supreme Court should hear cases that are "important to all Texans and provide consistency and predictability in the law."
Says appellate courts should be cautious about overturning jury verdicts.
Says "civility, professionalism, and respect are fundamental values" in the legal profession.
Said she does not want anyone to come into court thinking she will rule a certain way because she is a Democrat.

promises.text: Says she will "work to preserve every Texan's constitutionally embedded right to a trial by jury and respect for jury verdicts."

record.text: Was appointed to oversee two multidistrict litigation proceedings, including the lawsuits arising from the 2021 Astroworld festival.
Led the 11th District Court's operations during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Has presided over more than 200 trials since taking the bench in 2017, according to The Dallas Morning News.
In the Astroworld litigation she dismissed Drake from the lawsuits while keeping Apple Inc. and two of Travis Scott's companies as defendants, according to the Houston Chronicle.

notes.text: In the State Bar of Texas 2026 judicial poll, taken before the primary, Kristen Hawkins received 1,705 votes, Kyle Hawkins 1,203 and Gordon Goodman 674. The bar states the poll is not an endorsement.
The Dallas Morning News reported she has been favorably rated in the Houston Bar Association poll and is board certified in judicial administration.

The Dallas Morning News editorial board recommended her for Place 7; Wikipedia and Ballotpedia also list the Houston Chronicle, Austin Chronicle and San Antonio Express-News editorial boards and EMILYs List.
Endorsed by the Texas AFL-CIO, Bexar County Young Democrats, Liberal Austin Democrats and The Caucus.
Reported $301,668 cash on hand as of June 30, 2026; top donors included The West Law Firm ($35,000), and the Texas Tribune reported her donors are largely plaintiffs' firms and attorneys.
Won the March 2026 Democratic primary over former First Court of Appeals Justice Gordon Goodman with about 76 percent of the vote.
In 2024 the Houston Chronicle reported that more than half of respondents to the Houston Bar Association judicial evaluation rated her work excellent and another 21 percent very good.
Named Judge of the Year by the Texas chapter of the American Board of Trial Advocates for her work on jury trials during the pandemic.

q_textualism.summary: Replaces an earlier reported summary with her own questionnaire answer: she says neither label fits, that she considers the law's language, its intent when passed and the most reasonable construction, and that she is a pragmatist who values stare decisis and predictability.

q_judicial_selection.summary: Opposes moving to appointment, writing that it benefits political insiders and concentrates power, while noting that statewide judicial campaigns are costly and hard to communicate.

issue_notes.summary: Says she strongly supports the right to a jury trial and that appellate courts should be cautious about overturning jury verdicts.
Disagrees that the court is pro-business by design but says criticism stems from the court setting aside jury verdicts, which she says should happen only in limited circumstances.
Suggests blackout periods for all judicial candidates and says judges can decline contributions from parties with pending cases.

candidates.name: Brett Busby
candidates.current_role: Justice, Supreme Court of Texas, Place 8, since 2019
candidates.background: Busby lives in Austin. He graduated from Duke University and Columbia Law School and clerked for U.S. Supreme Court Justices Byron White and John Paul Stevens and for Judge Gerald Tjoflat of the Eleventh Circuit. He was an appellate litigator and partner at Bracewell in Houston and served on Houston's Fourteenth Court of Appeals from 2012 to 2018. Gov. Abbott appointed him to the Supreme Court in 2019; the Senate confirmed him unanimously and he won a full term in 2020.

priorities.text: Describes his approach as "applying our laws faithfully to all who come before the Court, never rewriting those laws from the bench."
Says "every decision must be grounded in the law, not politics, pressure, or personal preference."
Campaigns on expanding affordable legal help, saying "Access to justice must be more than a principle; it must be a reality."
Supports civic education through the Teach Texas program, which places lawyers and judges in seventh-grade classrooms.
Says he wants to improve the court's efficiency.

record.text: As the court's liaison to the Texas Access to Justice Commission, initiated the review that led the court in 2024 to give preliminary approval to rules licensing legal paraprofessionals and court-access assistants to give limited legal help.
Wrote the majority opinion in River Creek Development Corp. v. Preston Hollow Capital and joined the majority in State v. JRJ Pusok Holdings (June 2026).
Wrote more majority opinions, and more unsigned opinions for the court, than any other justice in fiscal year 2025, according to The Dallas Morning News.
Cited the court's 2026 majority ruling rejecting Gov. Abbott's request to remove Rep. Gene Wu as an example of the court ruling against the state's top elected officials.

Wrote the court's September 2024 opinion in In re Dallas HERO ordering three Dallas City Council charter propositions (K, M, and N) off the November 2024 ballot because their wording did not disclose that they conflicted with, and would control over, citizen-initiated charter amendments.

Wrote a 2024 concurrence, joined by Justice Lehrmann, in State v. Zurawski, joining the court's opinion that vacated a trial court's injunction concerning the medical-emergency exception to Texas abortion laws while stressing that the Legislature holds the power to limit abortion and must write abortion laws clearly and in explicit terms.

notes.text: In the State Bar of Texas 2026 judicial poll, taken before the primary, Busby received 1,913 votes and Gisela D. Triana 1,989. The bar states the poll is not an endorsement.
Named 2018 Appellate Judge of the Year by the Texas Association of Civil Trial and Appellate Specialists and received the 2022 Judicial Civic Education Award.
Endorsed by Gov. Greg Abbott, the Texas Civil Justice League and Texas Alliance for Life.
The Dallas Morning News editorial board recommended Busby, while describing both candidates as well qualified.
Before joining the bench he worked with the Federalist Society, Alliance Defending Freedom and First Liberty, according to the Texas Tribune.
Reported $1.3 million cash on hand as of June 30, 2026; top donors included Vinson and Elkins Texas PAC ($25,000) and Texans for Lawsuit Reform PAC ($25,000).
Unopposed in the March 2026 Republican primary.
Before joining the bench he represented a Florida inmate pro bono before the U.S. Supreme Court in Day v. McDonough (2006), which he says motivated him to seek a judgeship.

q_textualism.summary: Says he applies the law as written and respects its plain meaning because that produces more consistent, predictable rulings, and opposes rewriting laws from the bench.

q_judicial_selection.summary: Asked whether Texas should move to appointment, he urged Texans to consider the 2020 Commission on Judicial Selection, noting that a majority favored ending partisan judicial elections and many members recommended appointment followed by retention elections.

issue_notes.summary: Supports expanding legal aid, plain-language court forms and reducing regulations that raise the cost of legal services; called the legal profession's limited supply a factor in unmet civil legal needs.
Says he voluntarily follows the Judicial Campaign Fairness Act limits and declines contributions from parties with cases before his court.
Says the recent constitutional amendment giving non-lawyers a majority on the State Commission on Judicial Conduct and stiffening penalties seems likely to deter misconduct.

candidates.name: Gisela D. Triana
candidates.current_role: Justice, Texas Third Court of Appeals (Austin), Place 6, since 2019
candidates.background: Triana is from San Antonio and earned a bachelor's degree from the University of Texas at San Antonio and a law degree from the University of Texas. She worked as a staff attorney in the Secretary of State's Elections Division, as a prosecutor and criminal trial division director in the Travis County Attorney's Office, and in private practice. She served as a justice of the peace, a county court at law judge and, from 2005, judge of the 200th District Court before her election to the Third Court of Appeals. She was the Democratic nominee for this seat in 2020.

priorities.text: Says she has served at every level of the Texas judiciary and has seen how the system "can be improved at every level."
In her 2019 announcement, called for judges who "make independent decisions based on the rule of law" and a judiciary that "guarantees a level playing field."
Said in 2019 that the court needs "more balance" and diversity of thought.
Says she is the only candidate in the race with trial court experience and that jury verdicts should not be easily undone.

record.text: Has served on the Third Court of Appeals since 2019 after presiding over the 200th District Court from 2005, where she handled hundreds of complex civil cases.

Wrote a dissent from the Third Court of Appeals' denial of en banc review in Texas Department of Family and Protective Services v. Grassroots, a case over an emergency rule allowing detention centers to receive child-care facility licenses; she says the Supreme Court later agreed with her on standing.
Sat on the 2022 Third Court of Appeals panel that upheld an injunction allowing 19 school districts to require masks despite Gov. Abbott's order.
Wrote the Third Court of Appeals opinion upholding about $181,000 in sanctions against developer Nate Paul, according to Chari Kelly's campaign summary of Law360 coverage.
Says she authored more opinions than any other court of appeals judge in Texas last year and more than 800 opinions overall.

notes.text: In the State Bar of Texas 2026 judicial poll, taken before the primary, Triana received 1,989 votes and Brett Busby 1,913. The bar states the poll is not an endorsement.

In her 2020 race for the same seat, she said the all-Republican court was "result-oriented and beholden to special interests" and criticized rulings that allowed evictions and debt collections to resume during COVID-19.
The Dallas Morning News editorial board recommended Busby but described Triana as well qualified, "analytical, well-prepared and knowledgeable."
Endorsed by the Texas AFL-CIO, Liberal Austin Democrats, University Democrats and Panhandle Democrats.
Reported $128,786 cash on hand as of June 30, 2026, after raising $9,425 from January through June; most funds carried over from a previous campaign.
Unopposed in the March 2026 Democratic primary.
Endorsed by EMILYs List in May 2026.
Says she was named Judge of the Year by the Hispanic Issues Section of the State Bar of Texas.

q_textualism.summary: Says neither the textualist nor constructionist label fully fits, that the written text of the Constitution reigns supreme but should not be distorted, and that result-oriented outcomes should be called out.

q_judicial_selection.summary: Prefers an elected judiciary over gubernatorial appointment, which she says creates conflicts of interest, but says partisan elections are far from perfect and that nonpartisan elections might make more sense.

issue_notes.summary: Agrees the court is seen as pro-business and attributes this to its reversal of jury verdicts.
Supports more transparency and disclosure and more resources for the State Commission on Judicial Conduct, and favors recusal rules tied to campaign contributions and gifts.
