candidates.name: Katrina Pierson
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 33, since January 2025
candidates.background: Pierson is a communications executive and media strategist who served as national spokesperson for Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign and as a senior adviser to his 2020 campaign. She holds a bachelor's degree in biology from the University of Texas at Dallas and lives in Rockwall. She worked in health care administration and later founded a public affairs and crisis consulting firm. She won the seat in 2024 after defeating incumbent Justin Holland in a Republican primary runoff.

priorities.text: Campaigns on phasing out property taxes.
Says rapid growth is straining roads, water, schools and public safety, and favors stronger infrastructure, including the power grid and water supply.
Lists securing the border and elections as legislative priorities.
Lists academic excellence, parental rights, classroom discipline, school safety and expanded career and technical education as education priorities.
Lists protecting children and life and removing barriers to health care as priorities.

promises.text: Says she opposes taxpayer subsidies for private development and backs transparent planning for electricity, water, roads and emergency services for data centers and other large projects.

record.text: Voted for David Cook over Dustin Burrows in the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker of the House; Burrows won 85 to 55.
Voted for SB 2 in April 2025, creating a $1 billion education savings account program for private school and homeschool expenses; it passed the House 86 to 61.

Coauthored and voted for the House version of HB 2 (2025 school finance); she voted against concurring with Senate amendments, stating in the journal that the Senate lowered the House's basic allotment increase.
Voted for SB 1, the 2026-2027 state budget, in April 2025, stating in the journal that it funded border security, school choice, public schools and $51 billion in property tax relief.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), the hemp-derived THC products bill, on second reading; she was recorded absent on final passage.
Voted for SJR 5 (bail denial constitutional amendment) and SB 9 (bail procedures) in May 2025.
Voted against SB 31 (2025), which clarified medical exceptions to the abortion ban, explaining in the journal that its language could create a loophole.
Voted for SB 33 (2025), barring local government funding of travel for abortions, and for SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases by entities tied to certain foreign adversaries.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting enforcement of extreme risk protective orders in Texas.
Joint author of HB 4 (2025 congressional redistricting) and HB 7 (2025 restrictions on abortion-inducing drugs) in the second special session, and voted for both.
Authored HB 3560 (2025) on licensing of mental hospitals and mental health facilities, which became law.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2026-2027 budget in April 2025, which would have directed HHSC to seek a waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; it failed 63 to 85.
Voted for HB 5115 (2025), increasing the criminal penalty for election fraud; it passed the House 88 to 54.
Voted for SB 8 (2025), requiring certain sheriffs to enter agreements with ICE; it passed the House 86 to 47.

notes.text: Endorsed by Donald Trump, Ted Cruz and Greg Abbott, and by groups including the NRA, Gun Owners of America, Texas Alliance for Life and Texas Home School Coalition, according to her campaign site.

In September 2021 the U.S. House Select Committee investigating the January 6 attack subpoenaed her as one of 11 people tied to organizing the Ellipse rally; the cited account does not describe any charges.
Won the 2024 Republican primary runoff over incumbent Justin Holland, 56.4 percent to 43.6 percent.

q_prop_tax_eliminate.summary: Lists phasing out property taxes as a top legislative priority.

q_vouchers.summary: Voted for SB 2, the 2025 education savings account law, and cited full funding for school choice in explaining her budget vote.

q_school_funding.summary: Coauthored the House school finance bill and opposed the Senate version because it reduced the basic allotment increase.

q_ten_commandments.summary: Voted for SB 10 requiring classroom Ten Commandments displays.

q_abortion.summary: Voted for SB 33 and was joint author of HB 7 restricting abortion-inducing drugs, and voted against SB 31's clarified exceptions as too broad.

q_border_state.summary: Voted for the 2026-2027 budget and cited its border security and law enforcement funding as a priority; campaigns on securing the border.

q_bail.summary: Voted for SJR 5 and SB 9 in 2025.

q_cannabis.summary: Voted for SB 3, which would have banned most hemp-derived THC products, on second reading.

q_gun_laws.summary: Voted for SB 1362 barring enforcement of extreme risk protective orders and campaigns on defending gun rights.

q_water.summary: Lists strengthening water infrastructure as a legislative priority.

q_medicaid.summary: Voted against a 2025 budget amendment directing the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility to all groups eligible for federal matching funds; it failed 63 to 85.

q_election_fraud.summary: Voted for HB 5115 (2025) increasing the criminal penalty for election fraud.

q_deportation.summary: Voted for SB 8 (2025) requiring certain sheriffs to enter immigration enforcement agreements with ICE; no statement on deportation priorities was found.

issue_notes.summary: Says economic development must benefit existing residents and supports local input on large projects.

In 2023 voted for SB 14 (ban on gender transition treatments for minors), HB 2127 (state preemption of local regulations), SB 4 (state illegal entry offense) and SB 3 (border barrier funding).
Voted to impeach Attorney General Ken Paxton in May 2023; the House adopted the articles 121 to 23.
Voted for SB 1 (2021, second called session), the election law changes that passed the House 80 to 41.
Voted against HJR 102 (2023), a proposed constitutional amendment to let voters decide on legalizing sports wagering; the House adopted it 101 to 42.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2026-2027 budget in April 2025, which would have directed HHSC to seek a waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; it failed 63 to 85.

notes.text: Founded the Texas Freedom Caucus and has supported barring Democrats from House committee chairmanships.
Won close general elections in 2018 (by 391 votes) and 2020 (by 849 votes) before larger margins in 2022 and 2024.

q_gun_laws.summary: Voted for SB 1362 barring extreme risk protective orders.

candidates.name: Sandeep Srivastava
candidates.current_role: Real estate agent and small business owner
candidates.background: Srivastava is an Indian-born naturalized U.S. citizen, a real estate agent and small business owner who lives in the Plano and Frisco area. He holds a business degree and a master's degree in systems management and has served on boards of several North Texas Indian American community organizations. He ran twice for U.S. House District 3 without winning.

priorities.text: Campaigns on access to quality public education and saving public schools.
Campaigns on affordable health care and better health insurance access.
Lists reproductive freedom as a top challenge.
Supports lower property taxes and investment in schools and infrastructure.
Says he is committed to making home and auto insurance more affordable.

promises.text: Pledged to co-sponsor, vote for and defend a resolution seeking an Article V convention on congressional term limits.

Says he will support legislation to attract more insurers to Texas, incentives for disaster-resistant home upgrades and improvements to the Texas Windstorm Insurance Association to lower insurance costs.
Says he will work to fund school resource officers, threat detection technology and more school counselors.
Says he will push for transparency in insurance billing and protection from surprise medical bills.

notes.text: Won the March 2026 Democratic nomination unopposed.
In May 2026 a social media post mocking his English drew wide attention; his campaign condemned it and called on Rep. Shaheen to denounce the rhetoric. No statement from Shaheen was reported.

His campaign lists endorsements from Moms Demand Action (Gun Sense Candidate), Collin County Stonewall Democrats, Asian American Democrats of Texas, Plano Area Democrats, Frisco Democratic Club, Mental Health Now, The Hindu American PAC and the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, among others.

q_vouchers.summary: Calls for repealing voucher legislation.

q_school_funding.summary: Calls for increasing public school funding and raising teacher pay.

q_medicaid.summary: His campaign site supports exploring a state-managed Medicaid expansion with accountability measures and cost caps (replaces a stronger rating based on a third-party summary, since his own wording is conditional).

q_abortion.summary: Says medical decisions should be made by women and their doctors and lists reproductive freedom as a top challenge.

q_border_state.summary: Calls for ending Operation Lone Star so law enforcement can focus on criminal investigations.

q_gun_laws.summary: Designated a Gun Sense Candidate by Moms Demand Action, a group that backs background checks and red flag laws; no direct statement on gun laws was found.

issue_notes.summary: Supports nonpartisan, census-based redistricting by an independent commission.
Calls for grid weatherization and storage, and water conservation and reuse requirements with standards for large industrial users.
Supports transparency in property tax rates, limits on steep increases and more local voter control.
Proposes more insurer competition, state-backed incentives for storm-resistant homes, rate transparency and stronger state risk pools to lower home and auto insurance costs.
Supports investment in local law enforcement with accountability, community-based crime prevention, mental health and drug treatment programs, and more support for crime victims.

candidates.name: Jeff Leach
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 67, since January 2013; chair of the House Committee on Judiciary and Civil Jurisprudence
candidates.background: Leach is an attorney at Gray Reed in Dallas focusing on commercial litigation, construction and real estate law. He grew up in Plano and holds degrees from Baylor University and SMU's Dedman School of Law. He is serving his seventh term and chairs the Judiciary and Civil Jurisprudence Committee, and also serves on Public Education and Calendars.

priorities.text: Campaigns on property tax relief, citing the 2025 homestead exemption increases.
Campaigns on border security funding, including personnel, technology and barrier construction.
Campaigns on public education funding and teacher pay, citing HB 2.
Campaigns on protecting children, including keeping sexually explicit materials out of schools.
Campaigns on election security, including a constitutional amendment limiting voting to U.S. citizens.

record.text: Voted for Dustin Burrows in the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker of the House.
Voted for SB 2 (2025 education savings accounts); in 2023 he voted against the budget amendment barring voucher spending and against the amendment removing education savings accounts from HB 1.
Voted for HB 2 (2025 school finance); on the final concurrence vote he was recorded absent and entered a statement that he would have voted yes.
Authored HB 6 (2025), on school discipline management and student access to telehealth mental health services, which became law.
House sponsor of SB 12 (2025), on parental rights and restrictions on diversity, equity and inclusion programs in public schools; it passed the House 88 to 47.
House joint sponsor of SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in classrooms, and voted for it.
Primary author of HB 7 in the 2025 second special session, restricting the manufacture and provision of abortion-inducing drugs, which became law.
Voted for SB 3 (hemp-derived THC products), SB 17 (foreign adversary land), SB 8 (sheriff ICE agreements), SJR 5 and SB 9 (bail) and SB 1362 (extreme risk protective orders) in 2025.
Authored HB 4076 (2025), barring organ transplant discrimination based on vaccination status, which became law.
In 2023 voted for SB 14 (ban on gender transition treatments for minors), HB 2127 (state preemption), SB 4 (state illegal entry offense) and SB 3 (border barrier funding).
Voted to impeach Attorney General Ken Paxton in May 2023.
Voted for SB 1 (2021, second called session), the election law changes that passed the House 80 to 41.
Authored HJR 102 (2023), a proposed constitutional amendment to let voters decide on legalizing sports wagering, which the House adopted 101 to 42; it did not pass the Senate.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2026-2027 budget in April 2025, which would have directed HHSC to seek a waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; it failed 63 to 85.
Voted for HB 5115 (2025), increasing the criminal penalty for election fraud; it passed the House 88 to 54.

notes.text: Won the March 2026 Republican primary with 64.27 percent over Matt Thorsen, according to unofficial results.
After his 2023 impeachment vote, Paxton endorsed Leach's 2024 primary challenger Daren Meis; Leach won that primary with about 65 percent.
Endorsed by the Texas Association of Business PAC in October 2026.

In 2020 Leach contacted Collin College's president about a professor's social media posts criticizing Vice President Mike Pence; the professor was dismissed days later, and the college offered her a settlement in 2022.

q_medicaid.summary: Voted against a 2025 budget amendment directing the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility to all groups eligible for federal matching funds; it failed 63 to 85.

q_voting_access.summary: Voted for SB 1 (2021), which added new voting procedures and criminal penalties.

q_election_fraud.summary: Voted for HB 5115 (2025) increasing the criminal penalty for election fraud.

q_gambling.summary: Authored and voted for HJR 102 (2023), which would have let voters decide whether to legalize sports wagering.

issue_notes.summary: Cites SB 293 judicial pay raises and creation of 14 new district courts.
Supports requiring plans that cover gender transition care to also cover complications and detransition care.

candidates.name: Candy Noble
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 89, since January 2019
candidates.background: Noble is a former teacher and small family business owner with an education degree from Hardin-Simmons University. She has lived in Collin County for more than 30 years and lives in Lucas. She serves on the Human Services and Ways and Means committees and is president of the Texas Conservative Coalition. She previously served on the Texas Juvenile Justice Board.

priorities.text: Campaigns on using excess state revenue to buy down and eliminate the school maintenance and operations property tax.
Lists traffic from rapid growth and road capacity as a top challenge.
Lists protecting children and the elderly from predators as a top priority.
Says she will address flooding, power, water and road infrastructure.
Campaigns on limited government, public safety and business growth.

promises.text: Says she is seeking transportation funding for the district's roads.

record.text: Voted for David Cook over Dustin Burrows in the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker of the House.
Voted for SB 2 (2025 education savings accounts); in 2023 she voted against the budget amendment barring voucher spending and against the amendment removing education savings accounts from HB 1.
Voted for HB 2 (2025 school finance), including the final Senate version.
Primary House sponsor of SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms, which passed the House 82 to 46.
Primary House sponsor of SJR 37 (2025), the constitutional amendment stating that voters must be U.S. citizens, and of SB 33 (2025) on local government support for abortion travel.

Authored HB 22 (2025), exempting intangible personal property from property taxation, and HB 4211 (2025) on residential property interests controlled by certain entities, which her campaign describes as a response to the proposed EPIC City development; both became law.
Voted for SB 3 (hemp-derived THC products) in 2025, and cast the only no vote on the final HB 46 conference report expanding medical low-THC cannabis, which passed 138 to 1.
Voted for SJR 5 and SB 9 (bail), SB 17 (foreign adversary land), SB 8 (sheriff ICE agreements) and SB 1362 (extreme risk protective orders) in 2025.
Was excused for a family medical emergency during several August 2025 special session votes and entered statements that she would have voted for SB 8, HB 7 and SB 10.
In 2023 voted for SB 14 (ban on gender transition treatments for minors), HB 2127 (state preemption), SB 4 (state illegal entry offense) and SB 3 (border barrier funding).
Voted to impeach Attorney General Ken Paxton in May 2023.
Voted for SB 1 (2021, second called session), the election law changes that passed the House 80 to 41.
Voted against HJR 102 (2023), a proposed constitutional amendment to let voters decide on legalizing sports wagering; the House adopted it 101 to 42.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2026-2027 budget in April 2025, which would have directed HHSC to seek a waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; it failed 63 to 85.
Voted for HB 5115 (2025), increasing the criminal penalty for election fraud; it passed the House 88 to 54.

notes.text: Won the March 2026 Republican primary with 52.75 percent over Jeff Forrester and Freddie America, according to unofficial results.
Endorsed by Greg Abbott and Donald Trump; her 2026 primary opponent criticized her Paxton impeachment vote and cited an F rating from Texans for Fiscal Responsibility.
Endorsed by Texas Right to Life, Texas Alliance for Life, the Texas State Rifle Association and the NFIB, according to her campaign.
Won the 2024 Republican primary by about 5 points over Abraham George, a former Collin County GOP chairman.

q_prop_tax_eliminate.summary: Wants to use excess state revenue to buy down and quickly eliminate the school M&O property tax.

q_vouchers.summary: Voted for SB 2 and against 2023 amendments blocking vouchers; campaigns on passing school choice.

q_school_funding.summary: Voted for HB 2 and campaigns on its $8.5 billion in new funding and teacher pay raises.

q_ten_commandments.summary: Was the primary House sponsor of SB 10.

q_abortion.summary: Sponsored SB 33 and is endorsed by Texas Right to Life and Texas Alliance for Life.

q_border_state.summary: Says she fought to secure over $6 billion in border security funding; voted for 2023 barrier funding.

q_deportation.summary: Voted for the 2023 state illegal entry offense and says she supports deporting criminal illegal immigrants; no statement on those without criminal records was found.

q_bail.summary: Voted for SJR 5 and SB 9 in 2025.

q_cannabis.summary: Voted for SB 3 and was the only no vote on the final HB 46 medical cannabis expansion.

q_foreign_land.summary: Voted for SB 17 and highlights banning hostile nations from buying Texas land.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted for SB 14 in 2023 and highlights it on her campaign site.

q_gun_laws.summary: Voted for SB 1362 and is endorsed by the Texas State Rifle Association.

q_water.summary: Says she plans to address power and water infrastructure.

q_medicaid.summary: Voted against a 2025 budget amendment directing the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility to all groups eligible for federal matching funds; it failed 63 to 85.

q_voting_access.summary: Voted for SB 1 (2021), which added new voting procedures and criminal penalties.

q_election_fraud.summary: Voted for HB 5115 (2025) increasing the criminal penalty for election fraud.

q_gambling.summary: Voted against HJR 102 (2023), which would have let voters decide whether to legalize sports wagering.

issue_notes.summary: Says thousands of homes have been built along small two-lane roads and she is seeking state transportation funding.
Cites HB 142 strengthening the HHSC inspector general's ability to recover Medicaid overpayments.

candidates.name: Angie Carraway
candidates.current_role: Middle school social studies and history teacher
candidates.background: Carraway has taught middle school social studies and history for 14 years in the Lovejoy and Princeton school districts. She grew up in a military family, worked in hospitality as a young adult and was the first in her family to earn a college degree, from the University of North Texas. She has lived in Collin County for more than 20 years.

priorities.text: Campaigns on fully funding public schools and keeping teachers in classrooms.
Campaigns on lowering costs for housing, utilities, insurance and prescriptions.
Campaigns on transparent government and year-round engagement with constituents.
Supports protected defined-benefit pensions and cost-of-living relief for retired educators.

promises.text: Says she will work to end voucher programs and keep public dollars in public schools.
Says she will push to raise the state minimum wage to $15 an hour.
Says she will hold year-round town halls.
Says she will work to eliminate pharmacy benefit managers to curb prescription drug costs.
Says her first legislative priority is to immediately end education savings accounts and school vouchers.
Says she would raise the basic allotment by at least $1,000 per student and set a minimum teacher salary of at least $65,000, paid for with the state surplus.
Says she supports a state-funded, across-the-board pay raise for all educators and wants the state to match district contributions to TRS.

notes.text: Ran unopposed in the March 2026 Democratic primary.

Her campaign lists endorsements from Moms Demand Action (Gun Sense Candidate), McKinney Area Democrats, Mothers Against Greg Abbott, Save Our Public Schools, Collin County Democrats with Disabilities, Mental Health Now and Blue Horizon.

q_vouchers.summary: Says she would end voucher programs, which she says pull money from public schools.

q_school_funding.summary: Calls for fully funded public schools and fair teacher pay.

q_min_wage.summary: Supports raising the state minimum wage to $15 an hour.

q_gun_laws.summary: Told ATPE that improving school safety in the long term would require fundamental reforms to gun laws, and is designated a Gun Sense Candidate by Moms Demand Action.

issue_notes.summary: Wants to eliminate pharmacy benefit managers, which she says drive up drug prices.
Opposes the new through-year testing model under HB 8 and says test results should never be the sole factor in A-F ratings or used to penalize teachers financially.
Her campaign blog criticizes how the state education savings account program is run, including the vendor contract and the share of applicants already paying for private school.

candidates.name: Scott Brister
candidates.current_role: Chief Justice, Fifteenth Court of Appeals, since September 2024 (appointed by Gov. Greg Abbott)
candidates.background: Scott Brister is a Waco native with degrees from Duke University (1977) and Harvard Law School (1980), and he is board certified in civil appellate law, civil trial law and personal injury trial law. He presided over Harris County's 234th District Court from 1989 to 2000, served on Houston's First and Fourteenth Courts of Appeals (including as chief justice of the Fourteenth), and served on the Texas Supreme Court from 2003 to 2009. He was a partner at Hunton Andrews Kurth before Gov. Greg Abbott named him the first chief justice of the new statewide Fifteenth Court of Appeals.

priorities.text: Campaigns on establishing the Fifteenth Court of Appeals as a stable, principled statewide court.
Says he aims for consistent rulings in cases involving state government and business law.
Emphasizes clear legal writing and reasoned decisions.
Says every party deserves an impartial judge who applies the law, not personal beliefs or political preferences.
Campaigns on preserving public trust in the courts.

promises.text: Says he will follow the law as written and rule without regard to personal beliefs or politics.

record.text: Presided over the 234th District Court in Harris County from 1989 to 2000 and served on the First and Fourteenth Courts of Appeals from 2001 to 2003.
Served on the Texas Supreme Court from 2003 to 2009 after appointment by Gov. Rick Perry and election in 2004, writing 122 opinions for that court.

Wrote a dissent in the Texas Supreme Court school finance case Neely v. West Orange-Cove Consolidated ISD (2005), disagreeing with the judgment that the state's school finance plan was unconstitutional.
Chaired the Texas Commission on Public School Finance after a 2017 appointment by Gov. Greg Abbott.
Appointed by Gov. Greg Abbott in June 2024 as the first chief justice of the Fifteenth Court of Appeals, effective September 1, 2024.

Wrote the Fifteenth Court's August 2025 opinion dismissing Dallas County's suit against the Health and Human Services Commission over the backlog of mentally incompetent jail inmates awaiting state hospital beds; the Texas Supreme Court declined review in June 2026.

Filed a concurrence in December 2025 when the Fifteenth Court upheld an injunction blocking Attorney General Ken Paxton's reporting rules for large-county prosecutors, writing in substance that Paxton may request information in specific cases but may not impose blanket requirements.

notes.text: In the 1990s he posted the Ten Commandments in his Harris County courtroom and declined to remove them after being sued, according to the Texas Tribune.
The Fifteenth Court has ruled against Attorney General Ken Paxton in several high-profile cases, drawing public criticism from Paxton.

Bloomberg Law reported that he twice admonished lawyers from the attorney general's office over where and how the office files cases, including suits against Johnson & Johnson and Kenvue in small counties, and said both sides should be counseled toward professionalism.
State Bar of Texas 2026 Judicial Poll: Brister 1,957 votes, Jerry Zimmerer 1,594 (about 55 percent to 45 percent). The poll is a non-scientific survey of participating lawyers.
Endorsed by Gov. Greg Abbott, State Rep. Pat Curry and Texas Alliance for Life, and by the Texas Civil Justice League PAC.
Reported $228,242 cash on hand as of June 30, 2026; major donors included Texans for Lawsuit Reform PAC ($25,000).
The San Antonio Express-News recommended Brister and the other two incumbents, describing them as highly qualified and their work as generally viewed as independent of partisanship.

q_textualism.summary: Says judges are not lawmakers and should follow the law as written and respect the Constitution.

issue_notes.summary: Has said the rift between the attorney general's office and the court is unhealthy and that both sides should be counseled toward professionalism.

candidates.name: Jerry Zimmerer
candidates.current_role: Attorney; former Justice, Fourteenth Court of Appeals (2019 to 2024)
candidates.background: Jerry Zimmerer was elected to Houston's Fourteenth Court of Appeals in 2018 and served from 2019 through 2024. He has practiced in Houston in civil trial work, health law, cybersecurity and international commercial arbitration, and worked as a senior project manager and network engineer at AT&T Mobility from 2003 to 2015. He is a 1984 graduate of South Texas College of Law Houston and lists Bellaire as his city.

priorities.text: Campaigns on making the Fifteenth Court accountable to voters rather than to the officials who appointed its members.
Says judges deciding cases about state officials and agencies should owe nothing to the officials under review.
Says he would focus on court efficiency.
Says he would use the office to promote democratic values.
Campaigns on engaging working Texans, including labor groups, whose disputes with state agencies and public employers reach the court.
In 2020 he described his approach as being present, doing the job and following the law, and said only one of his nearly 300 opinions had been appealed to the Texas Supreme Court.

record.text: Elected to the Fourteenth Court of Appeals in 2018 and served from 2019 through 2024; lost his 2024 reelection bid.
Ran for the Texas Supreme Court in 2020 and lost the Democratic primary.

notes.text: State Bar of Texas 2026 Judicial Poll: Zimmerer 1,594 votes, Scott Brister 1,957 (about 45 percent to 55 percent).

Endorsed by the Bay Area Democratic Movement, Victoria County Democratic Party and Panhandle Democrats; iVoterGuide also lists the Texas AFL-CIO, Tarrant County Democratic Party and McKinney Area Democratic Club among his endorsers.
Has received endorsements from pro-LGBTQ+ and labor groups in Houston, according to the Texas Tribune.
Reported $15,142 cash on hand as of June 30, 2026.

In the 2020 Democratic primary for chief justice, the Texas Tribune reported that he criticized opponent Amy Clark Meachum for seeking to be the first woman elected to the post, and Meachum called his comments sexist.
The San Antonio Express-News recommended incumbent Scott Brister, writing that none of the Democratic challengers could match the incumbents' experience.

q_judicial_selection.summary: Argues the Fifteenth Court, whose seats were all filled by gubernatorial appointment, should answer to the law and to voters rather than to the officials who appointed it.

candidates.name: Scott K. Field
candidates.current_role: Justice, Fifteenth Court of Appeals, Place 2, since September 2024 (appointed by Gov. Greg Abbott)
candidates.background: Scott Field holds a political science degree from Texas A&M University and a law degree from the University of Texas School of Law. He clerked for Texas Supreme Court Justice Raul Gonzalez, practiced at Baker Botts and Butler Snow, and served on the Third Court of Appeals in Austin from 2013 to 2018. Gov. Greg Abbott appointed him the first judge of Williamson County's 480th District Court in 2022 and to the Fifteenth Court in 2024. He lives in Liberty Hill.

priorities.text: Campaigns on applying the law as written, not rewriting it to fit personal views or political outcomes.
Says Texans deserve a judiciary that is independent, even-handed and faithful to the Constitution.
Says every case deserves thoughtful, impartial review grounded in the law, not politics.
Promises impartiality, discipline and commitment to the rule of law.
Says judges must be humble about their role but bold enough to make decisions that may be politically unpopular.

promises.text: Says he will apply the law as written.

record.text: Served on the Third Court of Appeals in Austin from 2013 to 2018.
Appointed by Gov. Greg Abbott in 2022 as the first judge of the 480th District Court in Williamson County.
Appointed to the Fifteenth Court of Appeals, Place 2, effective September 1, 2024.

Wrote the Fifteenth Court's December 2025 opinion upholding an injunction against Attorney General Ken Paxton's reporting rules for large-county prosecutors, concluding that the Legislature did not expressly grant the attorney general rulemaking authority.
Joined Fifteenth Court rulings that drew Paxton's criticism, including one allowing Democratic legislators who left the state during the 2025 redistricting dispute to receive donations.

notes.text: Bloomberg Law reported that he called Paxton's public attack on the court shocking and said he follows the law as given regardless of who wins; it also reported that he interviewed in 2025 for a Texas Supreme Court vacancy.
During a February 2026 oral argument in a pending case involving a midwife and abortion, he described the state's evidence as very thin, according to Bloomberg Law.
Member of the Federalist Society and the Christian Legal Society.
State Bar of Texas 2026 Judicial Poll: Field 1,523 votes, Tom Baker 1,692 (about 47 percent to 53 percent).
Endorsed by Gov. Greg Abbott, The C Club of Houston and Texas Alliance for Life, and by the Texas Civil Justice League PAC.
Reported $287,492 cash on hand as of June 30, 2026; major donors included Texans for Lawsuit Reform PAC ($25,000).
The San Antonio Express-News recommended Field and the other two incumbents.

q_textualism.summary: Says judges should apply the law as written rather than rewrite it to fit personal views or political outcomes.

issue_notes.summary: Says he is passionate about the right to a jury trial and Texans' ability to exercise constitutional rights without government interference.

candidates.background: Chris Hill was first elected Collin County Judge in 2018 and is seeking a third term. He previously served as Collin County Commissioner for Precinct 3. He is a certified public accountant with degrees from Texas A&M University-Commerce, the University of Texas at Dallas, Webster University, and Columbia Biblical Seminary, and has worked as a corporate controller and an executive pastor. He lives in Collin County, where he says five generations of his family have lived.

priorities.text: Campaigns on the promise he says he first made of limited government, low taxes, and excellence in every aspect of county government.
Says he champions private property rights, limited regulation, and government transparency.
Points to his COVID-era record, summarized as no lockdowns, no closures, no mask mandates, and no vaccine mandates.
Says Collin County has one of the lowest county property tax rates in Texas.
Supports regional transportation planning and infrastructure coordination.

promises.text: Pledges to keep his promises and keep the county successful if re-elected to four more years.

record.text: On Sept. 14, 2026, he cast the lone vote against the county's $619.6 million fiscal 2026-27 budget and a tax rate of $0.151414 per $100 valuation, the county's first rate increase since 1993; both passed 4-1.

Before the September 2026 vote, his motion to cut each department's budget by 2.76 percent to avoid a rate increase failed, as did his motion to lower the employee pay target from the 75th to the 50th percentile of comparison counties.
In September 2026 he was the lone vote against an elected officials' compensation plan that included raises for him and the four commissioners.

On Aug. 25, 2025, he and Commissioner Cheryl Williams voted against the total tax rate and the maintenance and operations rate for fiscal 2025-26, and he also voted against the debt service rate; the rate stayed at $0.149343.
On July 31, 2024, he cast the lone vote against the proposed fiscal 2025 combined tax rate of $0.149343, which passed 4-1.

At a June 9, 2025 meeting he directed staff to plan a move to hand-marked paper ballots after a federal executive order on barcode tabulation; on June 23, 2025 the court unanimously approved about $2.3 million in equipment.
On March 24, 2020, he issued a seven-day COVID-19 stay-at-home order that, unlike many Texas orders, allowed businesses following social distancing rules to remain open.
As a county commissioner in May 2017, he made the motion, approved 4-0, to deny further invoice payments to the court-appointed special prosecutors in the Ken Paxton securities case.

On Aug. 10, 2026, the Commissioners Court voted 4-0, with Commissioner Duncan Webb absent, to call an $817.5 million bond election for Nov. 3, 2026, choosing the larger of two final options; with four members present, the unanimous vote included Hill.
On Feb. 23, 2026, he voted with a 5-0 majority to approve a consent agenda that included a construction change order for the jail's medical and mental health expansion.

In August 2021 the Commissioners Court, which he presides over, voted to commit all of the county's roughly $201 million in federal ARPA funds to three public health capital projects, including a medical and mental health infirmary at the county jail; the court documents reviewed do not record his individual vote.

In January 2022 the Commissioners Court approved by majority vote the establishment of the Collin County Mental Health Diversion Program as a mental health specialty court; the order does not record individual votes.

In February 2024 the Commissioners Court, by majority vote with Commissioner Duncan Webb absent, awarded the construction contract for the jail's medical and mental health expansion to Sedalco, Inc.; the order does not record individual votes.

notes.text: Won the March 3, 2026 Republican primary with 78.3 percent of the vote over former Plano council member Rick Grady.
The Dallas Morning News endorsed his opponent Rick Grady in the 2026 Republican primary.

His campaign site lists endorsements from groups including Texas Right to Life, Texas Values Action, the Collin County Association of Realtors, Texas Home School Coalition PAC, and the Texas Restaurant Association.
County records describe the ARPA-funded jail medical and mental health facility as 125 beds with shell space for 136 more, at a cost of about $112 million, with opening expected in late 2026.

q_county_tax.summary: Has voted against the county tax rate in multiple budget cycles and proposed across-the-board department cuts to avoid the 2026 rate increase.

q_spending_cap.summary: KERA reported that he argued the county budget had grown faster than inflation and population combined when proposing cuts in 2026.

issue_notes.summary: KERA reported that he warned raising the tax rate in the same year the county seeks voter approval of bonds could hurt the bond's chances; the court called an $817.5 million bond election for Nov. 3, 2026.
His campaign materials, as summarized by Branch Politics, say he supports regional cooperation on mental health services.
Opposes government health mandates and says public health decisions should prioritize personal liberty.
Says he supports school choice and homeschooling communities.

On the bond, Community Impact quoted him saying residents are "going to have to pay the bill, so we want their voice on this decision," and that deferred projects are pushed into the future; Hoodline reported he favored keeping the debt service rate steady.

candidates.name: Shelby Williams
candidates.current_role: Senior advisor, Endeavor Management; former Plano City Council member
candidates.background: Shelby Williams served on the Plano City Council, Place 5, from 2019 until he resigned in March 2025 to run for this open seat, held by Commissioner Duncan Webb, who is not seeking re-election. He was Collin County Republican Party chair until stepping down in April 2025. He holds an information technology degree from Western Governors University and an MBA from the University of Texas at Austin, and has worked in management consulting and digital marketing. He lives in Plano.

priorities.text: Campaigns on responsible taxation and budgeting, including fiscal roadmapping to plan for county needs years ahead.
Says water supply is one of the biggest issues facing the region and that infrastructure is not being built fast enough to keep pace with growth.
Campaigns on guiding growth by working with local governments, residents, businesses, and developers.
Says he will work with cities, the Regional Transportation Council, and TxDOT on congestion and road wear.
Calls public safety the top job of government and cites endorsements from the Plano and Dallas police associations.
Says roads, water, wastewater, fire coverage, and drainage must be in place before new rooftops, not after.
Says he will use relationships with mayors and council members to advise on consequential decisions before they are made.

promises.text: Says he will press for direct potable reuse and desalination, replace aging leaking pipe, and require data centers to use gray water rather than treated drinking water for cooling.
Said he would remain in the race to the end and would not use his party chair role in his campaign.
Says he will fund clinicians, detox capacity, and treatment courts so the jail's new Medical and Mental Health Facility operates as a program, not just a building.
Pledges funding for the county's Veterans Treatment Court.
Says he will make sure constables are properly equipped and funded and that county fire and EMS contracts deliver real coverage.

record.text: Branch Politics reports that during his time on the Plano City Council the city did not raise property taxes for four years.

Says that on the Plano council he championed a new comprehensive plan, limited additional apartments, led a streambank stabilization initiative, and backed a new fire training center and increased police funding.
Says he timed his March 2025 council resignation so the special election to fill his seat coincided with the May 2025 regular election.

notes.text: Won the March 3, 2026 Republican primary over Woody Huffines by 186 votes in unofficial results.

His campaign lists endorsements from Gov. Greg Abbott, Speaker Dustin Burrows, Sheriff Jim Skinner, District Attorney Greg Willis, Judge Chris Hill, Commissioners Darrell Hale and Susan Fletcher, the Plano Police Association, Dallas Police PAC, Texas Realtors PAC, and Texas Values Action.

q_county_tax.summary: Pledges to meet county needs in the most taxpayer-friendly way possible while also stressing that water and transportation infrastructure must keep pace with growth.

q_county_mental.summary: Says nearly a third of people in the county jail have a mental health disorder and says he will fight to fund clinicians, detox capacity, and the Veterans Treatment Court (corrects earlier wording that described a pledge of ongoing funding for treatment courts generally).

q_water.summary: Says water infrastructure is not keeping pace with growth and calls for direct potable reuse, desalination, replacing leaking pipe, and regional reservoir and aquifer projects.

issue_notes.summary: Cites North Texas Municipal Water District projections of a dry-year shortfall by the mid-2030s and supports regional cooperation on reservoirs, aquifer recharge, and interconnected water systems.
Supports expanding water distribution capacity and using nuclear power to increase energy capacity.
In an August 2026 post he wrote that bonds are the proper way to pay for long-lived assets and that "we need these bonds," while stressing that the bonds are a tax increase paid by taxpayers.
Says he favors the county acquiring land to dedicate as parks and open space, noting state law makes it hard to develop dedicated parkland.
Says the jail is overcrowded and that a shortage of detention beds is the reason for new jail construction.

candidates.name: Mike Missildine
candidates.current_role: Justice of the Peace, Precinct 3, since 2019
candidates.background: Mike Missildine was first elected Justice of the Peace for Precinct 3 in 2018 and is serving his second term. He previously worked in law enforcement with the Potter County Sheriff's Office, U.S. Border Patrol, campus police departments, and the Dallas County and Collin County constables. He holds a bachelor's degree in criminal justice from Midwestern State University and graduate degrees including a doctorate in psychology. He lives in Plano.

priorities.text: Says he has expanded court access through a 24-hour night drop box, evening dockets, and virtual hearings.
Says he plans extended evening office hours, a possible weekend court program, and online mediation to resolve cases without trial.
Says he supports the U.S. and Texas constitutions, free speech, gun owners' rights, and fair, speedy trials.
Says he will enforce state truancy laws equally while working with school districts to help families understand the value of education.
Says he will run the court efficiently using technology and common sense business practices.

record.text: His campaign says his court cut its case backlog from more than 33,000 to just over 17,000, reached a 173 percent clearance rate in fiscal 2024, and disposed of nearly 77,000 cases over four years; these figures are self-reported.

notes.text: Won the March 3, 2026 Republican primary with 65.5 percent of the vote over Danielle Sposito.
Faced Irvin Lynn Barrett in the 2022 general election as well.

His campaign lists endorsements from U.S. Rep. Keith Self, State Rep. Jeff Leach, County Judge Chris Hill, District Clerk Mike Gould, Commissioner-elect Michael Slaughter, and Constables Sammy Knapp, Matt Carpenter, and Dwayne Kurtz.
